prompt: Which is the best description of an inertial reference frame?
options: A frame at rest relative to the Earth
A frame moving at the speed of light
A frame moving at constant velocity, in which a body with no resultant force stays at rest or moves uniformly
A frame attached to a rotating object
markscheme: **C.** An inertial frame is one in which Newton's first law holds — it is not accelerating. A rotating merry-go-round (D) or braking car is non-inertial.

prompt: A student in a closed, windowless train carriage moving smoothly at constant velocity drops a ball and plays table tennis. Explain why no mechanics experiment inside the carriage can determine whether the train is moving.
markscheme: The carriage is an inertial frame **(R1)**; Newton's laws take the same form in all inertial frames, so every mechanics experiment gives the same results as in a stationary carriage (the ball falls straight down relative to the student) **(R1)**

prompt: Frame S′ moves at $20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ in the $+x$ direction relative to frame S; their origins coincide at $t=t'=0$. An event occurs at $x=500$ m, $t=10$ s in S. Find its coordinates in S′.
markscheme: $x'=x-vt=500-20\times10=300$ m **(A1)**; $t'=t=10$ s — Galilean relativity assumes absolute time **(A1)**

prompt:
**(a)** A ball is thrown forwards at $15\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ relative to a train moving at $20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. State its speed relative to the ground according to Galilean relativity. **[1]**

**(b)** Explain why the same rule fails for a light pulse emitted forwards from the train. **[2]**
markscheme:
**(a)** $35\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ **(A1)**

**(b)** Galilean addition predicts $c+20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ relative to the ground **(A1)**, but experiments (and Maxwell's equations) show light has speed $c$ in every inertial frame **(R1)**

prompt: State the two postulates of special relativity.
markscheme:
1. The laws of physics are the same in all inertial reference frames **(A1)**

2. The speed of light in a vacuum is the same, $c$, for all inertial observers, regardless of the motion of the source or observer **(A1)**

prompt:
Frame S′ moves at $0.60c$ relative to S along $x$; origins coincide at $t=t'=0$. An event has coordinates $x=3.0\times10^{8}$ m, $t=2.0$ s in S.

**(a)** Calculate $\gamma$. **[1]**

**(b)** Calculate $x'$ and $t'$. **[3]**
Two spacecraft approach each other, each moving at $0.80c$ relative to the Earth. Calculate the speed of one spacecraft measured by the other.
markscheme:
In the frame of craft A ($v=0.80c$), craft B has $u=-0.80c$ in the Earth frame **(M1)**

$u'=\dfrac{u-v}{1-uv/c^{2}}=\dfrac{-1.60c}{1+0.64}$ **(M1)** $=-0.98c$, i.e. speed $0.98c$ **(A1)** — less than $c$, unlike the Galilean $1.6c$.

prompt:
In frame S two events are separated by $\Delta x=6.0\times10^{8}$ m and $\Delta t=3.0$ s.

**(a)** Calculate the space–time interval $\Delta s$. **[2]**

**(b)** Hence determine the time between the events in a frame in which they occur at the same place. **[2]**
markscheme:
**(a)** $(\Delta s)^{2}=(c\Delta t)^{2}-(\Delta x)^{2}=(9.0\times10^{8})^{2}-(6.0\times10^{8})^{2}=4.5\times10^{17}\ \text{m}^{2}$ **(M1)**; $\Delta s=6.7\times10^{8}$ m **(A1)**

**(b)** In that frame $\Delta x'=0$, so $c\Delta t'=\Delta s$ (invariant) **(M1)**: $\Delta t'=2.2$ s — the proper time **(A1)**

prompt: A muon travels through the atmosphere. Which observer measures the **proper time** for the muon's lifetime and the **proper length** of the atmosphere?
options: proper time: muon frame; proper length: Earth frame
proper time: Earth frame; proper length: muon frame
markscheme: **A.** Proper time is measured in the frame where both events (creation, decay) happen at the same place — the muon's frame. Proper length is measured in the frame where the object is at rest — the Earth's frame for the atmosphere.

prompt: A particle has a proper lifetime of $2.0\ \mu\text{s}$ and moves at $0.80c$ relative to a laboratory. Calculate its lifetime measured in the laboratory.
A rod has proper length 10 m. What length does an observer measure when the rod moves along its length at $0.80c$?
markscheme: **B.** $L=\dfrac{L_0}{\gamma}=\dfrac{10}{5/3}=6.0$ m; only the dimension along the motion contracts.

prompt:
Two lamps 900 m apart in frame S flash simultaneously. Frame S′ moves at $0.60c$ along the line joining them, from the first lamp towards the second.

**(a)** Calculate the time between the flashes in S′. **[2]**

**(b)** State which flash occurs first in S′ and explain why observers disagree. **[2]**
markscheme:
**(a)** $\Delta t'=\gamma\left(\Delta t-\dfrac{v\Delta x}{c^{2}}\right)=-1.25\times\dfrac{0.60\times900}{3.0\times10^{8}}$ **(M1)** $=-2.3\times10^{-6}$ s **(A1)**

**(b)** $\Delta t'<0$: the flash from the second lamp (further along $+x$) occurs first in S′ **(A1)**. With $c$ the same in both frames, the time order of separated events depends on the frame; simultaneity is not absolute **(R1)**

prompt: On a space–time diagram with axes $x$ and $ct$ drawn to the same scale, the world line of a light pulse is:
markscheme: **C.** Light travels $\Delta x=c\Delta t$, so its world line makes $45^{\circ}$ with both axes. A stationary object's world line is vertical (parallel to the $ct$ axis).

prompt: The world line of a particle makes an angle of $30^{\circ}$ with the $ct$ axis. Calculate the particle's speed, and explain why no world line can make more than $45^{\circ}$ with the $ct$ axis.
markscheme:
$\tan\theta=\dfrac vc\Rightarrow v=c\tan30^{\circ}=0.58c$ **(A1)**

$45^{\circ}$ corresponds to $v=c$, and no massive particle can reach $c$ **(R1)**

concept: Muon decay as evidence for relativity
prompt:
Muons are produced 10 km above the ground and travel down at $0.995c$. Their half-life in their rest frame is $1.56\ \mu\text{s}$.

**(a)** Calculate the fraction expected to reach the ground if time dilation did not occur. **[2]**

**(b)** Calculate $\gamma$ and the fraction expected with time dilation. **[2]**

**(c)** Explain how the result is interpreted in the muon's rest frame. **[2]**
markscheme:
**(a)** Distance per half-life $=0.995\times3.0\times10^{8}\times1.56\times10^{-6}=466$ m; $10\,000/466=21.5$ half-lives **(M1)**; fraction $=2^{-21.5}\approx3\times10^{-7}$ **(A1)**

**(b)** $\gamma=10.0$ **(A1)**; dilated half-life $15.6\ \mu\text{s}$ → 2.15 half-lives, fraction $\approx0.23$ **(A1)**

**(c)** In the muon frame the half-life is the proper $1.56\ \mu\text{s}$, but the atmosphere is length-contracted to $10\,000/10.0\approx1.0$ km **(R1)**; the number of half-lives (2.15) and so the surviving fraction are the same — both frames agree on what is observed **(R1)**

Measurements show far more muons reaching the ground than (a) predicts, confirming (b).
